title: A speck of glass held up by a laser felt the kicks of single gas atoms
body: On 19 October 2026 physicists at Yale University reported in Physical Review Letters that they had felt individual gas atoms hitting a glass bead 100 nanometres across ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18371)). A focused laser held the bead in a vacuum chamber like a spring, so it swung to and fro along the beam 48,000 times a second, and light bouncing back off it tracked every swing. When the team let in traces of krypton, xenon or sulfur hexafluoride, each particle that bounced off changed that swing a little: a kick of momentum, mass times speed, which for the smallest kicks they could pick out, 200 keV/c in physicists’ units, changed the bead’s speed by about a tenth of a millimetre a second ([Science News](https://www.sciencenews.org/article/nanoparticle-tiny-impact-gas-atom)). In air, molecules hit a bead that size about 90 trillion times a second and blur into the jiggle called Brownian motion; in a near vacuum the hits come one at a time, so counting them measures the pressure. The group, led by David Moore, hopes such sensors will one day measure the emptiest vacuums and feel kicks from particles like neutrinos ([Physics World](https://physicsworld.com/?p=131173)).

slides.question: In air, about how many times a second do gas molecules hit a glass bead 100 nanometres across? Answer in trillions.
slides.explanation: About 91 trillion times a second, from the kinetic theory of gases for air at 20 °C. So many hits blur into a jiggle; in a near vacuum they come one at a time.

slides.alt: Animation in a dark vacuum chamber: a pink laser holds a glowing glass bead that swings along the beam, traced on a scope. Xenon atoms drift in; one bounces off and kicks the bead. A sum gives 177 keV/c, a scale shows kicks seen from 200, air molecules make it jiggle, and single kicks are counted.

slides.prompt: Pick xenon and let its atom bounce straight back. Find the slowest atom whose kick clears the 200 keV/c the experiment could pick out.
slides.takeaway: About 250 m/s: faster than xenon’s average of 217 m/s at 20 °C, which kicks only 177 keV/c. So the team caught the faster, more direct hits; an atom that sticks kicks half as hard.

slides.heading: Rank the kicks of particles bouncing straight back at their average speed
slides.note: Computed: kick = 2 × mass × average speed, for gases at 20 °C.
slides.explanation: Heavier particles move slower, but not by enough: at the same temperature speed falls as 1/√mass, so the kick still grows as √mass.

slides.heading: From a jiggle to single hits

events.text: Botanist Robert Brown reports tiny particles jiggling in water
Albert Einstein explains the jiggle as countless molecules hitting
Physicists catch a laser-trapped glass bead’s speed mid-jiggle
At Yale, single gas atoms’ kicks are felt one by one

slides.question: How could the Yale team use the levitated glass bead to measure the pressure of the gas in the chamber?
slides.explanation: More gas means more particles hitting the bead. The rate of kicks they counted gave the gas pressure, and it matched the chamber’s pressure gauge.

source.label: Tseng et al., Optomechanical Detection of Individual Gas Collisions (arXiv, Physical Review Letters, 2026)
